King Faisal. Faisal ibn Abdulaziz Al Saud was the third king of Saudi Arabia and a transformative figure in modern Middle Eastern politics. He became crown prince in nineteen fifty-eight and king in nineteen sixty-four, consolidating authority from his elder half-brother by promising modernization and religious credibility. Faisal oversaw Saudi Arabia's transformation into an oil superpower, using petroleum revenues to fund military expansion, infrastructure, and religious institutions. He led the oil embargo of nineteen seventy-three to nineteen seventy-four against the United States and other Western nations in retaliation for their support of Israel in the Yom Kippur War, demonstrating OPEC's geopolitical clout. Faisal promoted Wahhabism, the puritanical Islamic doctrine, as Saudi Arabia's state religion and exported it through educational and missionary networks across the Islamic world. He championed Arab unity and pan-Islamic solidarity while maintaining strong ties to the United States—a balancing act that defined Saudi foreign policy. He expanded the kingdom's military, patronized cultural projects, and advanced women's education, though cautiously within Islamic constraints. In March nineteen seventy-five, he was assassinated by his nephew, Faisal ibn Musaed, in a palace shooting; the motive remains disputed, but the deed shocked the region and reshaped the kingdom's trajectory, with Saudi Arabia remaining central to global energy politics and Middle Eastern affairs.
